name: Anthony Weaver

views.text: Coach players hard and then love them up; both halves matter.
A former player knows what a setback feels like and can talk a player through it.
Players see things on the field the booth cannot, so ask them how the calls should be taught.
Look for tough, competitive players first; scheme comes second.
Fourth-quarter collapses come from habits, and habits are fixed without blaming anyone else.
He coordinates to help his players win, not to audition for the next job.
A defense that is having fun plays faster and celebrates for each other.

signatures: draws on his seven playing seasons when talking a player through a slump
asks players for their input on calls and mentions it in public
admits when he has been on edge, then points to the habits that need fixing
want: to earn a head-coaching job on the strength of a defense that plays tough and loves its coaches
fear: that a bad defensive season defines him before he gets the chance to lead his own team
voice: Warm, direct and plain-spoken, with the credibility of a former player; he talks about players as people and about toughness as a standard. In bad stretches he stays deliberate, owns being on edge and refuses to blame others, with a little dry humor left in. He praises effort and connection more than scheme.

evidence.summary: Hiring release with his career: Ravens second-round pick in 2002, seven seasons with Baltimore and Houston, then college and NFL defensive line jobs, Houston defensive coordinator in 2020 and Ravens run game coordinator and assistant head coach 2021-23. Facts only.

As he leaves for Miami, John Harbaugh praises how he ran the defensive front, the pass rush and the run defense, calls him a leader and predicts he will be a head coach; notes his head-coach interviews with Washington and Atlanta. Team site; a warm send-off.

He says his playing career helps most in guiding players through setbacks, sums up his method as coaching hard and supporting personally, values players' in-game perspective, and looks for tough, competitive players in the Ravens mold. His own words at his introduction.

Camp feature: players call him genuine and relatable, a sharp change from Fangio; he gives players freedom and asks for input on calls, builds staff chemistry through pickup basketball, checks in on players' personal lives, and McDaniel stresses emotional connection. Player quotes; early-season optimism.

With the defense near the bottom of the league, he says he coaches to help players win rather than for advancement, admits being a little edgy, calls for mental toughness and no blaming, and ties fourth-quarter losses to habits under pressure. Writer describes him as deliberate but frustrated.
